newsitem.title: UK: Blair to announce Northern Ireland peace plan.
newsitem.headline: Blair to announce Northern Ireland peace plan.

text.p: New British proposals for peace in Northern Ireland to be made public on Wednesday by Prime Minister Tony Blair were given a cautious welcome by Sinn Fein, political arm of the IRA Irish republican guerrilla group.

But Sinn Fein signalled that it would need talks with London to clarify the proposals which Blair was to announce in parliament in the hope of breathing new life into the stalled Northern Ireland peace process.
Sinn Fein chairman Mitchel McLaughlin said that if the proposals resolved a long-running wrangle over disarmament, it would improve prospects for a new IRA (Irish Republican Army) ceasefire.
McLaughlin, in a telephone interview with Reuters, said Sinn Fein had not seen Blair's statement and its only knowledge was based on briefings, whose source he did not identify.
But he said Britain appeared to have largely accepted Sinn Fein's argument "that disarmament discussions should properly and legitimately take place alongside all other issues".
Asked about the possibility of Sinn Fein approaching the IRA for a new ceasefire in its campaign to end British rule in Northern Ireland, McLaughlin replied:
"We had four main areas of concern. If Tony Blair addresses them all this afternoon, we will have taken a giant step in that direction."
But McLaughlin stressed that clarity was needed and hinted that a further meeting would be needed with British officials.
"If we are to give leadership, we are entitled to know what the British prime minister's thinking is. It is a matter for the British to decide how we are going to get this elucidation."
But Blair's office was cool about Sinn Fein's request.

"I think we believe that all the qualification that is necessary is there (in the statement) and the prime minister is not prepared to go along with what he might feel is an attempt to string him along," said a close aide to Blair.

The key point of the plan which Blair drew up with outgoing Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, is "parallel decommissioning", a proposal made in January 1996 by George Mitchell, the former U.S. senator chairing the year-old peace talks.
The term means the IRA and its rival Protestant guerrillas would give up their arms in stages while talks proceeded.
Blair's predecessor, John Major, ousted in a May 1 election, was under severe pressure from the pro-British unionist politicians from Northern Ireland who shored up his tiny parliamentary majority.
With Blair's landslide victory, the Protestant politicians who want Northern Ireland to remain under British rule have lost much of the sway they held over the peace process.
David Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionists, said after talks with Blair on Tuesday that parallel decommissioning was not his party's "first preference."
But he said: "We indicated that we could go along...provided of course that that is what actually happened."
John Hume, head of the moderate pro-Irish nationalist SDLP, hailed the proposals on Tuesday. "I think a real and historic opportunity now exists to take the gun out of Irish politics for ever."
Hard-line Democratic Unionist Party leader Ian Paisley, however, has accused London and Dublin of having "given in to the IRA" and said his party might quit the all-party talks.
Sinn Fein's request for talks poses a problem for Britain.
A week ago the IRA shot dead two policemen in the town of Lurgan in County Armagh, throwing peace hopes into disarray and provoking Britain to cut off contacts with Sinn Fein.

In a new incident on Wednesday, bomb disposal officers in Lurgan were preparing to examine "a suspicious object" after an overnight explosion in a car park while a British security forces patrol was in the area. No one was hurt.
